tip_title: Cold Weather Is Coming. One Plumbing Scenario Your Home Policy Handles — and One It Doesn't.
topic: Home Insurance - Water Damage Sudden vs. Gradual (Winter Prep Angle)
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Cold Weather Is Coming. One Plumbing Scenario Your Home Policy Handles — and One It Doesn't.**

Standard homeowners policies cover sudden and accidental water damage — a pipe that bursts unexpectedly overnight is a covered loss in most cases. What they don't cover is gradual damage: a slow drip under a cabinet that went unnoticed for months, or a pipe that failed because it was never insulated and froze every winter. Insurers treat that second scenario as a maintenance issue, and maintenance issues are excluded. The distinction matters a lot right now because temperatures are about to start dropping, and a frozen or neglected pipe in an unheated space is exactly the kind of loss that gets denied.

Before the first real cold snap, it's worth checking any exposed pipes in attics, crawl spaces, or garages — and making sure they're insulated. That's not just good home maintenance. It's also how you protect a future claim.

Not sure what your policy covers for water damage? Your Peachy agent can walk you through the specifics.

📖 [Learn more from NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/homeowners/learn/does-homeowners-insurance-cover-water-damage)
summary: Covers the sudden-vs-gradual water damage distinction in homeowners policies framed around fall-to-winter pipe freeze risk — specifically that frozen/neglected pipes are treated as a maintenance exclusion, distinct from prior tips on the sudden-vs-gradual rule in a summer/rain context.
scoring_notes: October is the right timing for winter pipe-freeze prep in Georgia and North Texas. Prior tips on sudden-vs-gradual water damage were framed around summer neglect scenarios — this is a substantively different angle tied to seasonal temperature change and freeze risk. Both audiences have high homeownership (78% East Cobb, 55% Perimeter, 65% Lewisville Lake) with meaningful home coverage stakes. Actionable: readers can check pipe insulation this week. tip_title: October Is Actually One of the Riskier Months for Your Car. Here's Why.
topic: Auto Insurance - Comprehensive Coverage Fall Hazards
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: October Is Actually One of the Riskier Months for Your Car. Here's Why.**

Most people think of fall as a low-drama season for driving. But October brings a real spike in non-collision damage — deer are in peak movement during rut season, hail storms still roll through the South and Midwest well into fall, and wind events send tree limbs and debris onto parked cars more than people realize. All of that falls under comprehensive coverage, which is a completely separate part of your auto policy from collision. If you only have liability and collision, none of those events are covered — not the deer, not the hail, not the branch that lands on your hood overnight.

Pull up your policy or your declarations page and confirm comprehensive is listed. It's typically one of the cheaper coverages to add, and October is exactly when you want it in place.

Not sure what's on your policy right now? Your Peachy agent can pull it up and walk you through it in about five minutes.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/what-is-covered-by-collision-and-comprehensive-auto-insurance)
summary: Covers comprehensive auto coverage as the protection that applies to fall-specific non-collision damage (deer strikes, hail, wind debris), framed as an October action item to confirm comprehensive is on the policy before peak exposure hits.
scoring_notes: October is genuinely peak season for deer strikes and fall storm events. Both audiences have meaningful auto exposure. Prior tips on comprehensive covered summer road trips and hurricane-season context — this is a fresh angle tying comprehensive specifically to fall/October hazards (deer, wind debris, late-season hail). Trusted source (iii.org). Works equally well for East Cobb, Perimeter, and Lewisville Lake audiences — all suburban/exurban with real deer and storm exposure.
